extraction.research_question: How has the cryptocurrency lobby, led by the super PAC Fairshake, shaped the 2024 US election and subsequent policy, and does the sector's trajectory from decentralized anarchism through statism to oligarchy mirror Marxian historical materialism? (pp. 4-6, 11)
extraction.theory: Marxian historical materialism, applied as a stage model: cryptoanarchism (bands), then statism (city-states), then oligarchy (concentrated capital and power). Also draws on the co-optation of retail "YOLO capitalism" by institutional and oligarchic actors (pp. 11-15).
extraction.data: No dataset, sample, unit of analysis, or N. The quantitative content is a handful of press-reported or self-reported figures: Fairshake raised $203 million for the 2024 cycle (p. 7); Fairshake claims 253 pro-crypto candidates supported in 2024 (p. 8); $78 million raised toward the 2026 midterms to date (p. 9); "100,000 crypto millionaires" with no source in the text (p. 14). Sources cited are press and news items (refs 9, 28, 30, 34). Period covered: roughly 2008 to early 2025.
extraction.method: Qualitative narrative essay. It combines descriptive reporting of campaign-finance and election events with conceptual argument. No statistical estimation, no coding scheme, no comparison group, and no formal test.
extraction.identification: None. The paper makes no causal claim tested by an identification strategy. Its claims that Fairshake "decisively" influenced outcomes (pp. 9-10) are asserted, not estimated.
extraction.scope: Population: the US cryptocurrency industry and its federal political activity, mainly the 2024 federal election cycle. Institutions: super PACs (Fairshake, Protect Progress, Defend American Jobs), Congress (a House-passed digital-asset bill, Senate pending), and federal regulators (SEC, CFTC). Era: 2008 to early 2025, with the 2024 election as the focal event. Also comments briefly on non-US jurisdictions (El Salvador, China), without analysis.

The paper asserts Fairshake's campaigns against Katie Porter (California Senate primary) and Jamaal Bowman (NY re-election) show it can 'influence electoral outcomes decisively'. No outcome counterfactual or estimate is offered.

summary_md:
Chohan's discussion paper is an essay, not an empirical study. It describes Fairshake, the crypto super PAC network that also includes Protect Progress and Defend American Jobs, and argues that the industry has moved from crypto-anarchism through statism to an 'oligarchic' stage, using a Marxian stage model. Its numbers come from the press or from Fairshake itself: $203M raised for the 2024 cycle (p. 7), 253 supported candidates with no win rate and no counterfactual (p. 8), $78M already raised toward 2026 (p. 9), and an unsourced count of 100,000 crypto millionaires (p. 14). It names targeted races: Moreno over Brown in Ohio, against Tester in Montana, against Porter in a primary and against Bowman. It says these show 'decisive' influence (pp. 9-10) but estimates nothing, and it notes that many of the ads never mentioned crypto (p. 8).

For Paul's systems the paper adds no measurement or method. Its value is descriptive, and it points the same way in three places.

1. **Crypto money flows mostly through super PACs.** It is corporate-treasury money aimed at elections and often spent against candidates, not PAC contributions to candidate committees. That fits Mentat keeping a separate Super PAC channel and a support/oppose field. It also shows that Melange's flip model cannot see this money at all, because its industry money term counts only direct bank and finserv PAC receipts.
2. **The series breaks in 2024.** A new entrant spent at record scale in its first big cycle, which supports the registry decision to decline a crypto forecast for now.
3. **Primary-contest plays exist in practice.** Industry money has been used to contest primaries, the same kind of play the electoral-plays module models.

None of the paper's claims about effects on outcomes can be used as evidence. That applies especially to the competitiveness multiplier, where reciprocity is still not validated.

gaps_exposed: Melange's flip and money-response models do not include super PAC independent expenditures. They see only direct PAC contributions to members ('banks' and 'finserv'). For an industry like crypto that spends mainly as outside money, competitor pressure is invisible to the engine.

The model has no deterrence or spillover term. In the paper's account, punishing a visible opponent such as Brown or Tester is a signal to other members. The engine's money terms act only on the member who receives the money.
Mentat keeps the attributed beneficiary estimate unbuilt, so crypto corporate-treasury money routed through super PACs cannot yet be tied to candidate-level support or oppose totals.
Crypto stays declined in the forecast registry. A cycle-phase method has no way to handle a new entrant whose first big cycle is a level break.
flags: The 'decisive influence' claims (pp. 9-10) and the 253 'supported' candidates (p. 8) have no denominator, no window beyond '2024', no win rate and no counterfactual. Do not quote them as effect evidence, and do not cite them as support for the competitiveness multiplier: reciprocity is NOT validated (D-104..D-108).

Every dollar figure is press-reported or self-reported ($203M, $78M) or unsourced (100,000 millionaires). Any reuse must name the source and the window (2024 cycle; 2026 to date as of about Jan 2025) and treat the figures as unverified against FEC.
The paper's 'oligarchy' and influence framing is normative. Do not carry that language onto staffer or revolving-door edges or into graph ranks (D-025).
The paper makes no SNA proposal and no LDA edge use, so it does not trigger the rejected-proposal or D-021 flags.
paul_alignment: Paul has not annotated this paper, and none of his positions cite it. It sits closest to his margin note on Kim J. 2025, 'I may need to take into account the presence of conflicting industries', and to his wish to map rival-industry champions. The paper confirms that crypto is now a large, separately organized electoral actor. But it shows that actor working through super PAC spending rather than lobbying filings or bill positions, which is a channel his conflicting-industries idea and the Melange money engine do not yet model. The paper is also the kind of confident ROI and influence narrative that Paul's own evidence tests (the sector-growth study, the competitiveness lane) have not borne out, so it should not raise his confidence in money effects.

extraction.title: Big Five Personality Predictions From Twitter Using Regression
extraction.venue: SSRN (ssrn.com/abstract=5213216); authors affiliated with Computer Science & Engineering, MIET College, Meerut. No journal or conference named.
extraction.document_type: Working paper / preprint (SSRN). Short proposal-style paper with no reported empirical results.
extraction.coverage: Read the full text file (559 lines, about 19,959 characters) in one pass, covering front matter, abstract, introduction, literature review, methodology (3.1-3.6), conclusion and references 1-21. The text extraction contains only the captions of Figures 1-5, not the figure contents. Paul's markup: no markup files were listed for this work, so none were read. Metadata hint corrected: the title, authors and SSRN 5213216 match the text; the text states no year or venue.
extraction.research_question: Can the Big Five personality traits of a Twitter user be predicted automatically from their tweets using NLP, sentiment analysis and machine learning/regression, as a scalable alternative to questionnaire-based assessment? (Abstract; Section 1.) The text never states a formal hypothesis.
extraction.theory: Big Five trait model, which the paper labels as "Creativity, Dependability, Sociability, Kindness, and Anxiety" (Sections 1-2, 3.3). These labels are non-standard: the conventional Big Five are Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness and Neuroticism. Section 2 itself refers to "agreeableness and neuroticism", so the labelling is internally inconsistent. The paper also draws on the claim that linguistic cues and sentiment link to personality traits (Section 2), citing a Facebook meta-analysis at "[14]".
extraction.data: The paper describes a planned data pipeline, not an analysed dataset. Tweets are collected via the Twitter API using keywords, hashtags and user handles; fields include tweet text, user info, timestamps and interactions (Section 3.1). The system takes a Twitter handle and a user-specified number of tweets (Section 1). Unit: presumably one user's tweet set. Sample size (N): not reported. Time period: not reported. Source of trait labels for training: not stated ("Tweets are labelled according to personality traits using models like the Big Five", Section 3.3). No dataset name, size or download source is given.
extraction.method: Pipeline (Sections 3.1-3.6): (1) cleaning, removing URLs, mentions, hashtags, lowercasing and stopword removal; (2) tokenization; (3) TF-IDF vectorization, plus LIWC and other psycholinguistic features; (4) user profile features (follower count, tweet frequency, bio); (5) sentiment analysis of positive and negative tone; (6) classifiers named as Random Forest, Neural Networks and SVM (Section 3.3), and elsewhere Naive Bayes, SVM, RNN or BERT (Section 3.5 text), with supervised regression to output a percentage per Big Five trait (Sections 1, 3.5, Figure 5). Training uses cross-validation to limit overfitting. Evaluation uses accuracy, precision, recall and confusion matrices (Section 3.4). Feature importance is analysed (Section 3.5). The results are visualised as pie charts (Abstract; Section 4). Regression is described only in words and in Figure 5 (caption only). The paper contains no equations beyond the TF-IDF formula caption (Figure 2).
extraction.identification: None. The paper is a predictive pipeline with cross-validation. It makes no causal, quasi-experimental or instrumental claim, and no identification strategy is stated.
extraction.scope: Population: Twitter users generally, with English-language tokenization implied (Section 3.2 discusses English word boundaries). No demographic, country or language restriction is stated. Institution: a student engineering project at MIET College, Meerut (CSE department). Era: not stated. The paper's references run to 2024, so the work is presumably from around 2024-2025. Generalisability: not discussed beyond cultural-context future work.

key_findings.finding: The paper claims a machine learning approach can predict Big Five traits from Twitter data via sentiment analysis, with results shown as percentage pie charts.
Regression is used to output each Big Five trait as a percentage per user.
key_findings.location: Section 1 (paragraph on the model); Section 3.5 final bullet; Figure 5 caption

key_findings.finding: Classifier choice (Random Forest, Neural Networks, SVM) is justified by stated effectiveness only; no comparison is run.
Model accuracy, precision and recall are said to be measured with cross-validation and confusion matrices. No values are reported.
The abstract claims the model reveals health-related indicators such as stress levels. No method, label or result for stress appears in the body.
The paper concludes the approach is more efficient and scalable than questionnaires, and that it suits business and mental-health uses. No comparison data is shown.
A personalised video link giving advice on personality improvement is described as a unique feature. Its design, content and evaluation are not described.

measures: Sentiment: positive and negative sentiment scores per user (Sections 1, 3.2)
TF-IDF term weights (Section 3.2, Figure 2)
LIWC emotional and cognitive word categories (Section 3.2)
Psycholinguistic features (Section 3.2, truncated)
User profile features: follower count, tweet frequency, bio (Section 3.2)
Big Five trait percentages as regression outputs (Sections 1, 3.5)
Classification evaluation: accuracy, precision, recall, confusion matrix (Section 3.4)
Feature importance (Section 3.5)
limitations: The authors state no limitations section. The text gives only future-research items: refine models for diverse cultural contexts and address data privacy and ethical concerns (Section 4; ethics also in Section 2).
No sample size, data period, label source or validation results are reported, so the claimed accuracy cannot be assessed.

Trait labels are non-standard (Creativity, Dependability, Sociability, Kindness, Anxiety) and do not match the conventional Big Five names used in the paper's own Section 2, which cites agreeableness and neuroticism.
Classifiers and regression are both named, but the regression target and how training percentages were obtained are never explained.
Model lists are inconsistent between Section 3.3 (Random Forest, NN, SVM), Section 3.5 (Naive Bayes, SVM, RNN, BERT) and the conclusion (SVM and deep learning).
Several in-text citations do not match the reference list. For example, the Facebook meta-analysis is cited as [14], which is a GeeksforGeeks page. Reference [3] shares its title with this paper.
Several references are to blog or tutorial pages, and some URLs look like placeholders (e.g., a Medium URL ending in 123456789). This weakens the evidentiary basis of the literature review.
references_of_note: Stachl et al. (2020), 'Predicting personality from patterns of behavior collected with smartphones', PNAS 117(30):17680-17687 (ref 5). Behavioural-sensing personality prediction; the closest real-data work cited.

Wang et al. (2018), 'Sensing behavioral change over time: within-person variability features from mobile sensing to predict personality traits', ACM IMWUT 2(3) (ref 10). Behavioural sensing, not text.
Jia (2018), 'Mental health computing via harvesting social media data', ASMMCMMAC'18 (ref 13). Social-media mental-health link; relevant to the paper's stress claim.

Patel et al. (2017), 'Analyzing Personality Traits from Social Media Content: A Case Study with Facebook Data', ICCSE (ref 12). Likely the source for the Facebook-behaviour claim, but cited in text as [14], which is a different source.

No reference in the list addresses lobbying, legislators, elections, persuasion, turnout, networks, path-finding or allocation. Interaction networks are mentioned only in passing (Section 2).

summary_md:
**What the paper is.** This is a short SSRN proposal from a student engineering group at MIET College, Meerut. It describes a pipeline that would take a Twitter handle, clean and tokenize the tweets, and build TF-IDF, LIWC-style, sentiment and profile features (follower count, tweet frequency, bio). A classifier or regression would then output each Big Five trait as a percentage, shown in a pie chart. The paper reports no sample size, no data period, no source for its trait labels, and no accuracy figures. The model list changes between sections. The trait names are non-standard ("Creativity, Dependability, Sociability, Kindness, Anxiety"), and several citations do not match the reference list. The abstract's claim about stress detection has no method behind it. In short, this is a design sketch, not evidence.

**Why it matters here, and how little.** The only component it touches is Melange's lexical Big Five reader. That reader already does more than the paper proposes: LIWC-analog rates, Mairesse SMOreg weights, a refit to RKH targets, token-based low-confidence shrinkage, and reported held-out CV (mean .350 across the five traits, window and N as recorded in the brain). The project's validation record goes further still. The pre-registered nomological look rated lexical Big Five as unfit for behavioural prediction, and receptivity now runs on a behavioural basis. The paper offers nothing that could test or recalibrate any of this, and none of its features should be adopted on its authority. Two cautions transfer. First, its profile features (follower count, tweet frequency) are volume proxies of the kind the system has already rejected. Second, it outputs absolute "percentages" with no reference norm, while the system deliberately reports traits as z-scores relative to its own corpus. Read it as a negative example of an unvalidated trait-from-text claim, not as support.

bearings.paper_claim: Proposes predicting Big Five trait percentages from tweets with TF-IDF, LIWC/psycholinguistic categories, sentiment and profile features, using RF/SVM/NN (Sec 3.3) or NB/SVM/RNN/BERT (Sec 3.5) plus regression. No N, no label source and no accuracy, precision or recall values are reported. It says cross-validation and confusion matrices are used (Sec 3.4) but shows none.
bearings.system_side: A closed-vocabulary LIWC-analog reader (rates per 1000 words, with low-confidence flags below 1,500 tokens), weighted by Mairesse SMOreg and refit to RKH targets. Traits are z-scored relative to this corpus only. Held-out CV against RKH: E .510, A .406, C .363, ES .258, O .214. The system already implements, and has measured, the feature family the paper only proposes.
bearings.transfer_conditions: It does not transfer as evidence. There are no labels, no sample, no results, and the genre (general Twitter users) differs from legislators' floor speech and interviews. At most it is a list of candidate features. Its absolute 'percentage' outputs conflict with the system's rule that scores are meaningful only within this corpus. Its accuracy claim stays unverified and should never be cited as a benchmark (DE-062 spirit).

extraction.year: 2017 per the metadata hint; the text itself shows no year (its latest cited work is Madsen 2016)
extraction.venue: Not stated in the text. Page numbers run 2651 to 2656, which suggests a proceedings or journal volume, but no venue name appears.
extraction.document_type: Peer-reviewed academic paper (simulation study with an agent-based model). The text does not label the article type.
extraction.coverage: Full text read in two chunks (lines 1 to 694 of the extracted text, about 34,400 characters), including abstract, introduction, model, simulation design, results, discussion and references. extraction.research_question: Does a micro-targeted campaign (MTC), which contacts only voters with a favourable view of the candidate's credibility, persuade the electorate more efficiently than a stochastic campaign that contacts voters at random? Can an agent-based model with a Bayesian source-credibility belief-updating rule simulate persuasion campaign strategies? The paper frames itself as an exploratory proof of concept.
extraction.theory: Bayesian source-credibility model (Harris et al., 2015; Bovens & Hartmann, 2003; Hahn et al., 2009/2012). Credibility is split into expertise (E, capability to give accurate information) and trustworthiness (T, willingness to give accurate information). The two are treated as orthogonal. Beliefs are revised with an expanded Bayes rule, p(h|rep), using conditional probabilities from Table 1 taken from Madsen (2016), so belief revision has no free parameters. Political campaign theory: the persuasion phase of a campaign is modelled separately from get-out-the-vote (Green & Gerber, 2008). Micro-targeting background draws on Issenberg (2012) and O'Neil (2016).
extraction.data: No empirical data. The study is a simulation. Units are simulated voters (agents). N = 10,000 voters per simulation, 2 candidates, 1 binary proposition (H = 0 or 1), 50 ticks (campaign days). Voter expertise and trustworthiness scores are drawn from normal distributions with mean 0.5 or 0.6 and SD 0.25. Voter prior belief is drawn from normal (mean 0.5, SD 0.25), bounded 0.01 to 1. The MTC candidate's reach is fixed at 20 contacts per tick. The non-MTC reach ratio runs from 1 to 10. The text does not report the number of replications or random seeds. The conditional probability table (Table 1) is garbled in the extraction, with values 80.38, 58.21, 34.63, 18.04, 22.59, 42.3, 59.90, 71.26 and no clear units.
extraction.method: Agent-based model (ABM) with two agent types, voters and persuaders. Persuaders are either MTC or stochastic (non-MTC). Voters are randomly distributed, with no spatial role, and have no links to each other. Persuaders make direct contacts. The non-MTC candidate contacts voters at random and states p(candidate) = 1. The MTC candidate contacts only voters whose signal factor (mean of T and E) exceeds 0.5, sampling randomly among eligible voters up to its reach, and states p(candidate) = 0. Each contacted voter replaces its belief with the posterior P(candidate|rep). A voter is contacted at most once per tick. At the end, each voter votes for the candidate it favours (p > 0.5). Design: 2 x 2 manipulation of mean credibility (0.5 or 0.6) crossed with non-MTC reach ratio 1 to 10. Outcome is the share of voters supporting the non-MTC candidate. Results are presented as a single figure (Fig. 2). No statistical tests, confidence intervals or sensitivity analysis are reported.
extraction.identification: None in the causal-inference sense. The mechanism is built in by design: the MTC selection rule and the Bayesian update are fixed, and the two manipulated inputs are credibility mean and reach ratio. The authors frame the study as a proof of concept and do not claim identification of real-world effects.
extraction.scope: Population: a simulated electorate of 10,000 homogeneous-process voters. Institution: a stylised two-candidate, single-proposition election with a persuasion phase only. Turnout is not modelled, since all voters vote with probability 1 at the end. Era: not stated. The model is motivated by contemporary micro-targeting in US-style campaigns, citing Issenberg (2012) and O'Neil (2016). The model does not include negative campaigning, multiple issues, voter networks or personality differences.

key_findings.finding: Under the Bayesian source-credibility rule, an MTC with the same reach consistently beats a stochastic campaign.
key_findings.numbers: MTC reach fixed at 20 per tick; non-MTC reach ratio 1 to 10 (ratio 1 = equal reach). Exact vote shares are only in Fig. 2 and are not given in the text.

key_findings.finding: With mean credibility 0.5, a stochastic (non-MTC) campaign is inefficient. Opinions are equally split, so blind contacts reach supporters and opponents in equal numbers. Blind campaigns only work when the candidate's average perceived credibility is above 0.5. Below that, they can be ineffective or harmful.
A non-MTC campaign with roughly double the reach cancels out the MTC advantage.
key_findings.numbers: Break-even at non-MTC reach about 2x the MTC reach (MTC reach = 20).

key_findings.finding: If the non-MTC reach ratio exceeds 2 and the non-MTC candidate's perceived credibility is above 0.5, the stochastic campaign beats the strategic one.
Discussion restates that the MTC advantage is not general: a positively perceived stochastic candidate with greater reach can beat a strategic one.
key_findings.numbers: Non-MTC needs double reach to cancel the advantage.

key_findings.finding: The authors predict, without testing, that MTC efficiency rises with available voter data and with electorate complexity (belief systems, individual differences, voter-to-voter interaction). MTC costs are also predicted to rise with complexity.
key_findings.numbers: None reported; this is a prediction only.

limitations: The authors call the study exploratory. The model is 'necessarily simplified' and a 'proof of concept' (p. 2651, p. 2655).
Voters are cognitively homogeneous, with the same belief-revision process. There are no moral foundations, personality or reasoning-strategy differences (p. 2655).
Voters consider a single proposition, while real elections involve many issues, preferences and candidates (p. 2655).
The MTC segments only on candidate favourability, not on swing/secure status, policy preference or turnout likelihood (p. 2655).
Voters cannot communicate or influence one another. Social networks, community leaders and social nodes are absent, though the authors suspect MTCs would do better with them (p. 2653, p. 2655).
Real campaigners do not get a perfect signal from each voter. Noise was added to the voter signal, but the amount and form of that noise are not described in the text (p. 2655).
Turnout is not modelled. All voters vote with probability 1 at the end (p. 2652).
The conditional probabilities are taken from Madsen (2016) and not calibrated to this electorate (p. 2653).
No replications, confidence intervals, statistical tests or sensitivity analysis are reported. Results rest on one figure (Fig. 2).
Negative campaigning is not implemented (footnote 3, p. 2654), and the model is not tested against real campaign data.
Footnote 2 and the Table 1 layout are garbled in the extracted text, so the conditional-probability values cannot be checked against the printed table with confidence.
measures: Share of voters who favour the non-MTC candidate at end of campaign (y-axis of Fig. 2).
Non-MTC reach ratio, non-MTC reach divided by MTC reach (x-axis; 1 to 10).
Mean perceived credibility of each candidate (0.5 or 0.6), with SD 0.25 for the trustworthiness and expertise draws.
Voter signal factor: the mean of trustworthiness and expertise, with threshold 0.5 for MTC contact.
Voter prior belief p(candidate), drawn from normal (mean 0.5, SD 0.25), bounded 0.01 to 1.
Posterior belief P(candidate|rep) after each contact, from the Bayesian source-credibility formula with Table 1 conditionals.
references_of_note: Harris, Hahn, Madsen & Hsu (2015), The Appeal to Expert Opinion: a Bayesian Network approach, Cognitive Science 40. Source of the credibility-revision formula used here.
Bovens & Hartmann (2003), Bayesian Epistemology. Foundation for integrating source reliability into Bayesian belief revision.
Hahn, Oaksford & Harris (2012), Testimony and argument: a Bayesian perspective. Source-reliability background.
Madsen (2016), Trump supported it?! A Bayesian source credibility model applied to appeals to presidential candidates' opinions, CogSci. Source of Table 1 and the empirical validation claim.

Duggins (2016), A Psychologically-Motivated Model of Opinion Change with Applications to American Politics, arXiv:1406.7770. Only prior ABM work on political opinion cited, and the authors say it did not model campaign strategies.
Quattrociocchi, Caldarelli & Scala (2014), Opinion dynamics on interacting networks: media competition and social influence, Scientific Reports. Cited for future network extension.
Watts & Dodds (2007), Influentials, Networks, and Public Opinion Formation, Journal of Consumer Research. Cited for hierarchy and influentials in network opinion dynamics.
Issenberg (2012), The Victory Lab. Background on micro-targeted campaigns in practice.
O'Neil (2016), Weapons of Math Destruction. Background on data-driven voter segmentation.
Green & Gerber (2008), Get Out the Vote. Source of the persuasion versus get-out-the-vote campaign phase distinction.
Epstein & Axtell (1996), Growing Artificial Societies, and Parunak, Savit & Riolo (1998), Agent-Based Modeling vs. Equation-Based Modeling. Methodological basis for the ABM approach.

summary_md:
Madsen and Pilditch build a small agent-based model as a proof of concept. Two candidates compete over 50 ticks for 10,000 simulated voters who are not connected to each other. Each contacted voter replaces its belief with a Bayesian source-credibility posterior. Credibility is split into expertise and trustworthiness, and the conditional probabilities come from Madsen (2016) with no free parameters. The micro-targeted campaign contacts only voters whose mean credibility score for it is above 0.5, 20 per tick. The stochastic campaign contacts voters at random, with reach set to 1 to 10 times the targeted campaign's.

Results:
- At equal reach, targeting wins.
- When mean credibility is 0.5, random contact is wasted, because contacts land on favourable and unfavourable voters in equal numbers.
- A random campaign with about twice the reach cancels the targeting advantage.
- Above a 2x reach ratio, and with credibility above 0.5, the random campaign wins.

All results come from one figure. The paper reports no replications, no intervals and no sensitivity analysis, and it does not model turnout, multiple issues, or voter-to-voter networks.

For Paul's systems this is weak evidence about mechanism, not a calibration source. It agrees with two design choices: contacts go only to receptive targets, and money is never spent trying to convert opponents. Both match the paper's finding that blind contact with low-credibility audiences is inefficient or harmful. It also says the advantage of targeting depends on reach, which no part of the system models. The closest analogue is Terrier's untapped-potential score for door canvassing. That score gives persuasion weight to undecided likely voters but carries no credibility or receptivity term for the messenger. That missing term is the variable that decides the paper's result. The paper does not touch the cosponsorship network, LDA, reciprocity, or the rank pillars. It gives no reason to change a constant. Every number it reports is a simulation output, not an estimate.

bearings.paper_claim: Persuasion contact with voters who give the messenger credibility at or below 0.5 is inefficient or harmful. Targeting only receptive voters (signal factor above 0.5) beats random contact at equal reach; random contact needs about 2x the reach to break even. Simulation only: N=10,000 agents, 50 ticks, targeted reach 20 per tick.
bearings.system_side: potential = (wp x (1-|2s-1|) x t + (1-wp) x s x (1-t)) x (1 + wi x i). The persuasion weight peaks for undecided likely voters (s = 0.5). The formula has no term for how credible the canvasser or candidate is to the person being contacted, and no term for backfire.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Partial transfer. Both concern voter-level persuasion targeting in a two-candidate race. The paper, however, uses unconnected simulated agents, a single proposition and no turnout, and its credibility values are drawn from distributions, not measured. It supports adding a messenger-credibility or backfire guard as a hypothesis to test against canvass results. It does not support any particular weight. Strength is weak because these are uncalibrated ABM outputs with no replications reported.

bearings.paper_claim: Under Bayesian source-credibility updating, contacts restricted to receptive targets (credibility signal above 0.5) convert better than untargeted contacts. Contacting audiences who view the source unfavourably moves them away from the source's position.
bearings.system_side: gate(n) = max(0.15, seed_prob x SGATE[tier]). SGATE falls from 1.00 for Highly Persuadable to 0.35 for Opponent, so the system already expects contacts with unreceptive targets to convert at lower rates. The model has no negative (backfire) outcome for a contact.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Directional agreement only. The paper's agents are voters, not legislators. Its unit is a source-credibility belief update, not a take-up decision about cosponsoring, and it estimates no take-up rates. The SGATE values remain unestimated design constants; this paper does not calibrate them.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-influence-engine#Contingent seed activation gate|Contingent seed activation gate]]

bearings.paper_claim: Contact spent on audiences with an unfavourable view of the source is wasted or counterproductive. The targeted campaign's advantage comes entirely from never contacting those voters.
bearings.system_side: Members whose overall tier is Skeptic, Highly Skeptical or Opponent receive zero money in every allocator, which funds allies instead of trying to convert opponents. The gate fails open for members with no matrix row.
bearings.transfer_conditions: An analogy only. Campaign contacts with voters are not PAC dollars to legislators, and the paper has no money mechanism. It agrees with Paul's Furnas reading ('cultivate champions') but adds no new evidence about legislator behaviour.

gaps_exposed: Terrier's untapped potential has no messenger-credibility or backfire term. In the paper, the share of the audience that views the source favourably is the variable that decides whether contact helps or hurts.

No component models the trade-off between reach and targeting: how much more random reach makes up for targeting precision (the paper's break-even is about 2x). The allocators and turf planner treat contact capacity as a fixed budget, not a strategy choice.
None of the influence-engine contact models (SGATE, PERS) has a negative outcome for a contact. A contact with an Opponent only converts with low probability; it never pushes the member further away.
flags: The paper's results are simulation outputs from a single figure, with no replications, intervals or sensitivity analysis reported. None of its numbers (the 0.5 credibility threshold, the 2x break-even reach) should be quoted as empirical estimates or used to set SGATE, PERS or Terrier weights. If cited, it should be labelled as a theoretical proof of concept.
Per DE-062, this agent analysis is UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it.

The paper does not argue for either SNA proposal this project has rejected (dropping regular cosponsorship edges; per-edge volume normalization). It has no network at all, so there is nothing to flag there.
paul_alignment: Paul has not annotated this paper. It agrees with his Furnas-based position that ideological money cultivates champions rather than recruiting them, and with his seeding view taken from Chen et al. (contingency-aware seeding: legislators may or may not move when approached). Both are already built as the stance money gate and SGATE. His Broockman & Kalla and Kalla & Broockman highlights on the door canvass are about how the message is delivered. This paper adds a different dimension: who the messenger is to the voter. Terrier's potential formula encodes neither. Nothing in his notes is out of date relative to this paper.

related.why: Tappin measures persuasive returns to microtargeting with experiments; Madsen and Pilditch only simulate them. Tappin is the empirical check on this paper's claim that targeting has an advantage.
Simchon also studies the persuasive effects of political microtargeting, with generative-AI messages. It offers the empirical evidence this paper does not have.
Both make contact conditional on the target's receptivity. Chen does it as contingency-aware seeding, which the system implements as SGATE; this paper does it as credibility-gated contact.
A two-candidate competitive voter-dynamics model on networks. It adds the voter-to-voter interaction this paper leaves out and says targeting would benefit from.

backlinks.why: An agent-based model of micro-targeted campaigning. Issue-specific, voter-position-dependent responses of the kind measured here are the empirical input such a model would need.

Both build agent-based simulation models of a political process (micro-targeted campaigning in Madsen; knowledge brokering in state agencies here), so they are the vault's two ABM references for any future agent-level extension of the influence engine.
Item file title matches Madsen and Pilditch 2017, an agent-based proof of principle for micro-targeted campaigning; this paper supplies the field-experimental counterpart with net-of-cost numbers.

extraction.title: Strategic identity signaling in heterogeneous networks
extraction.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), vol. 119, no. 10, e2117898119; published March 3, 2022
extraction.document_type: Journal article: empirical test with a behavioral experiment, plus a formal payoff model
extraction.coverage: Full text read: the extracted text file was re-read in full this run (1305 lines, 78,765 chars, pages 1-10, including front matter, abstract, significance, introduction, results, discussion, Materials and Methods, and references). The item file ext, which said 18 bytes and blank, is stale; the text file now holds the full paper. Metadata hint title confirmed; authors, year, venue and DOI were empty in the item and are filled from page 1. Paul markup: all 47 annotation records were read (page 1: 26, page 2: 21; 42 yellow and 5 green; dated 2026-06-01). None carries covered text or a note, and the text file has no coordinates, so the highlighted passages cannot be recovered; only position and colour are reported. Dropped from paul_markup: 7 yellow page-2 highlights (file indices 35-41, y 322-563), because of the 40-item cap; the 5 green highlights were kept. No SI, OSF data or figures were available; SI results are cited only as the paper cites them. Not relevant to any bearing: no bearings were requested.
extraction.research_question: Do people strategically switch from overt to covert political identity signals (signals readable by ingroup but obscured from outgroup) depending on the share of outgroup members in their audience and on the cost of being disliked? (p.3, lines 309-314 and 320-323)
extraction.data: Three linked samples. (1) Twitter: 73,869 follower lists of 8 news accounts; 16,398 engaged seed accounts (top 20 percent by media diet); 1,834 far-left and 1,446 far-right accounts labelled homogeneous or heterogeneous; 6,594 tweets, 5,215 randomly sampled for rating, 4,752 rated by at least 3 raters per group; tweets downloaded September 15 to October 12, 2020 (p.8-9). (2) Raters: 2,695 invited Mechanical Turk workers, 1,992 responded (483 far left, 533 moderate left, 461 far right, 515 moderate right); each rated 50 tweets (p.9). (3) Behavioral experiment: 240 far-left/right and 240 moderate participants recruited (p.9), analysed as n = 481 (238 copartisan audience, 243 cross-partisan audience, Fig. 5); each saw 40 same-side tweets over 8 rounds. Unit: tweet and participant-round. Period: experiment September 15 to November 1, 2020 (p.8). Note the 480 recruited vs 481 analysed gap is not explained in the text. Data and code: OSF doi 10.17605/OSF.IO/XMZRA, anonymized (p.8).
extraction.method: Covertness is measured by rating differences: tweets are marked potentially covert when copartisan raters show a large difference in perceived orientation and affect (five criteria, SI Table S6), moderates give neutral orientation and affect, and far copartisans recognise political content; potentially overt tweets use four criteria (p.9). Selection: about 30 candidates per category, then 20 tweets in each of covert left, covert right, overt left and overt right, chosen by author judgement (p.9). Experiment: between-subject audience type (copartisan vs cross-partisan) and within-subject randomized 8 rounds varying outgroup size (1, 4, 6 or 9 of 10) and cost of dislikes (0.5 or 1 cent) (p.9). Analysis: mixed-effects Poisson models of covert and total tweets shared per round, random intercepts per individual, controls for age, gender, race, education and political group; average predictive margins and average marginal effects via the Spost13 package; Bayes factors for null effects from BIC differences (p.5). Mathematical model: expected payoffs of pure overt and covert strategies, with reception probabilities R, r_I and r_o, calibrated to the experiment, then plotted as a payoff advantage over outgroup share d (p.4, Fig. 4). Rater reliability: multilevel regression with Shapley decomposition of McFadden pseudo-R2 (p.9).
extraction.scope: United States only. Twitter users identified as politically engaged far-left or far-right, selected by news diet. Experiment participants are politically engaged, social-media-literate Americans across the spectrum, selected via the SI criteria (p.5). Time window: 2020 pre-election period, including the Black Lives Matter protests, Barrett confirmation and the 2020 election, with signals mostly about cross-partisan disputes (p.2, p.6, p.7). Political identity treated as left-right, unidimensional (p.8).
extraction.theory: Covert signaling theory (Smaldino, Flamson and McElreath 2018; Smaldino and Turner 2021): identity signals are accurately received by ingroup but obscured from outgroup; covert signalling is favoured when interactions with dissimilar others are likely and costly (p.2, lines 174-189). Linked to audience design and multiple-audience theory (Clark and Schaefer; Fleming and Darley) and to identity signalling (Donath; Berger) (p.2, p.7).
extraction.identification: The Twitter stage is observational: covertness is inferred from ingroup-outgroup rating gaps, not from the author intent. The experiment is randomized: audience group, outgroup size and cost are manipulated within subject across rounds, with random ordering (p.9). Authors state they cannot separate signaler intent from receiver understanding (p.7).
measures: Perceived political orientation of tweet author, 7-point scale from extreme left to extreme right, or not political (p.8)
Affective response: how much raters liked the tweet and how offensive it would be to similar people, summed (r = 0.70 between the two) (p.8)
Covert and overt classification from the five and four criteria (p.9)
Likes and dislikes from audience members per round; bonus of 1 cent per like and cost of 0.5 or 1 cent per dislike (p.3, p.9)
Number of covert tweets shared and total tweets shared per round; proportion covert (p.5, p.6)
Outgroup size: 1, 4, 6 or 9 of 10 audience members (p.9)
Political group: far left, moderate left, moderate right, far right, from news diet, self-report and views on radical movements (p.8)
Network heterogeneity: engagement of followers with copartisan far-left or far-right news accounts (p.8)
key_findings: Cross-partisan audiences: moving from 1 to 9 outgroup members raised the number of covert tweets shared, controlling total shared, with AME 0.73, 95 percent CI 0.47 to 0.99 (p.5, Fig. 5B).
Under high cost, moving from 4 to 6 cross-partisan outgroup members gave AME 0.42, 95 percent CI 0.08 to 0.77 (p.5).
Copartisan audiences (moderate vs radical): no effect of outgroup size on covert tweets; Bayes factor for null BF01 = 43.15 (p.5, Fig. 5A).
Cost of dislikes: no strong effect on the outgroup-size relationship; BF01 = 16.83; maximum payout gap only 20 cents (p.5, p.6-7).

Participants shared fewer tweets overall as cross-partisan outgroup size rose: AME -5.38, 95 percent CI -6.04 to -4.72; the authors read this as cutting overt tweets while keeping a few covert ones (p.6, Fig. 5D).

Audience reception: covert tweets were liked less by copartisans and disliked less by cross-partisans than overt tweets, but covert tweets did not eliminate outgroup dislikes (p.3-4, Fig. 3, n = 481).

Calibrated model: receiving probabilities R = 0.8 (overt), r_I = 0.6 (covert, ingroup) and r_o = 0.5 (covert, outgroup), against the prior-model assumption r_o = 0; covert payoff advantage is positive only when the outgroup share is high (p.4, Fig. 4).
Model predicts the outgroup-share effect should be much larger than the cost effect; experiment matched this, with the cost effect smaller than expected (p.4-6).
Rater reliability: multilevel model explains 50.0 percent of total variance; 89.3 percent of that is tweets, raters 10.3 percent of explained variance (5.2 percent of total) (p.9).
Strategy change paid: cross-partisan participants who shifted toward covert tweets with more outgroup members received higher bonuses (SI Fig. S8, cited p.5).

Political groups differ slightly: copartisan right participants used slightly more covert tweets; the moderate-to-radical gap was larger on the right; far-right participants changed strategy least (p.6-7). The authors could not explain these with groups this small.
Observational check: a greater fraction of political tweets from heterogeneous networks were classified as covert than from homogeneous networks (SI Fig. S5, cited p.9).
limitations: Network heterogeneity is operationalised by engagement with copartisan extreme news, because cross-partisan follower ties were rare and cross-partisan embeddedness practically nonexistent (p.8).
Covertness is inferred from rater reactions, not from author intent or receiver understanding; the authors say they cannot discern intent (p.7).
Covert and overt are treated as a dichotomy in design but are likely continuous and heterogeneously distributed (p.7-8).
The cost manipulation (max 20 cents) may be too small to change behavior, so the cost prediction is not supported (p.6-7).
Experiment fixes audience composition and gives no feedback between rounds; networks do not co-evolve with signalling (p.7).
Only a left-right dimension is used; participants could not signal about other identities (p.8).
Authors chose the final 20 tweets per category by judgement after automated preselection; two right-leaning tweets were wrongly included as covert and recoded as neither (p.9).
Experiment ran in the 2020 pre-election period when cross-partisan disputes dominated; copartisan null may reflect the period (p.6).
Rater noise: raters explain 5.2 percent of total variance (p.9); the paper reports reliability as high.
Recruited 480 participants but analysed 481, unexplained in the text (p.5, p.9).
Participants may have maximised payoff rather than shared identity; the design does not capture a genuine identity-sharing motive (p.7).
Automated political-speech classifiers are likely to detect only overt speech and miss covert signals (p.7).

summary_md: van der Does, Galesic, Dunivin and Smaldino (PNAS 2022, 119(10) e2117898119) test covert signaling theory: people send identity signals that the ingroup reads but the outgroup cannot, and do so more when the audience is mostly outgroup. They built a tweet set of covert and overt left and right messages from rater gaps (1,992 MTurk raters; tweets from 2020), then ran a randomized 8-round experiment (n = 481 analysed) that varied outgroup size (1 to 9 of 10) and the cost of dislikes. With cross-partisan audiences, going from 1 to 9 outgroup members raised covert sharing (AME 0.73, 95 percent CI 0.47 to 0.99) and cut total sharing (AME -5.38). Copartisan audiences showed no effect (BF01 = 43.15), and the cost manipulation did little (BF01 = 16.83). A calibrated payoff model (R = 0.8, r_I = 0.6, r_o = 0.5) puts the covert advantage only at high outgroup share. The authors warn that automated political-speech classifiers probably catch only overt speech. For Paul's systems, the paper bears on the stance and press layers, not the network. Members facing mixed audiences may hedge, go quiet or code their messages, so the press pillar and the DEBATE stance reader could understate them. The say-do gate only lowers tiers, so it cannot correct for members who act more than they talk. The salience-shock backfire term ignores audience composition. Every transfer is UNVERIFIED (DE-062). The subjects were ordinary partisan Twitter users on a left-right axis, not legislators speaking about a largely bipartisan credit-union agenda. This paper offers nothing on graph edges, weights or reciprocity. An earlier relation pass said the text was blank; that result is stale, because the text file now holds the full paper (78,765 chars).

extraction.title: Competitive Influence Maximization in Social Networks
extraction.document_type: Theoretical computer science paper (conference-style; inferred from "full version due to space constraints" and the Proc. citations; the text does not state venue or year)
extraction.coverage: Full text read in one pass (text lines 1-336, all of 16802 chars), including abstract, introduction, model, best-response analysis, first-mover analysis, tree FPTAS, proofs, acknowledgments and references. Some proofs (Lemma 3, Lemma 4 is given; Lemma 3 deferred) and the directed-line and arborescence extensions are stated as deferred to a full version and are not in this text.
extraction.research_question: How do multiple players (companies or innovations) competing by viral word-of-mouth choose initial seed sets in a social network under a generalized independent cascade model? Specifically: best responses to an opponent's strategy, the efficiency of equilibria ("price of competition"), first-mover strategies in a two-player duopoly, and whether single-player influence maximization admits an FPTAS on bidirected trees.
extraction.theory: Independent cascade model of diffusion (Goldenberg et al.; Kempe, Kleinberg, Tardos), extended to multiple competing colors. Motivated by Hotelling's model of competition and by competitive facility location and Voronoi games (text lines 47-48). Uses submodular utility systems (Vetta) and submodular maximization via greedy (Nemhauser, Wolsey, Fisher).
extraction.data: None. Purely theoretical analysis; no sample, unit of analysis, time period, or N is reported.
extraction.method: Formal model definition with exponentially distributed activation delays and random color tie-breaking (Section 2, lines 63-85). Best-response analysis via a deterministic equivalent of the random process and proof of monotone submodularity of expected reach (Lemma 1, Section 3). Approximation via greedy for submodular maximization. Equilibrium efficiency via Vetta's utility-system theorem (Section 3). First-mover analysis on lines via dynamic programming over a cutoff point c, with Lemma 2 (optimal solution cuts each line into equal pieces) (Section 4). FPTAS for bidirected trees via dynamic programming over subtree values G(v,k,q+,q-) with probability rounding at granularity delta = epsilon/n^3 and an inductive error bound (Theorem 3, Section 5).
extraction.identification: Not applicable. No empirical identification strategy; results are worst-case approximation and proof-based guarantees.
extraction.scope: Population, institution, and era: none. Scope is abstract graphs: directed graphs G=(V,E) with edge activation probabilities; two-player duopoly for first-mover results (Section 4); multi-player game for best response and price of competition; bidirected trees for the FPTAS (with the extension to bounded treewidth claimed but not shown).

key_findings.finding: Best response to fixed opponent strategies: player i's expected reach is a monotone and submodular function of S_i, so greedy gives a (1-1/e) approximation to the best response for the last player to commit.
key_findings.location: Section 3, Lemma 1 and Theorem 1 (abstract lines 15-16; intro lines 51-52; proof lines 92-120)

key_findings.finding: Price of competition (uncoordinated equilibria vs. single controller with all seeds) is at most 2, via Vetta's utility-system theorem applied to the total activated set, which is monotone submodular in the union of seeds.
Game has no pure-strategy Nash equilibrium in general, but mixed-strategy Nash equilibria exist.

Two-player first-mover game on disjoint lines: the optimal solution cuts every line into equal-sized pieces, so the red player need only try n*k candidate cutoff values l_i/j (i=1..n, j=1..k), giving a strongly polynomial dynamic program.
key_findings.location: Section 4, Lemma 2 and paragraph at lines 149-153
key_findings.numbers: n*k candidate cutoff values; lines of lengths l_1..l_n; k cuts

key_findings.finding: FPTAS for single-player influence maximization on bidirected trees, including unequal probabilities in opposite edge directions: a 1-epsilon approximation, with rounding granularity delta = epsilon/n^3 and additive error at most delta*n^3 <= epsilon <= epsilon*OPT.
key_findings.location: Section 5, Theorem 3 and the closing paragraph after its proof (lines 176-231)
key_findings.numbers: delta = epsilon/n^3; approximation 1-epsilon; additive error <= epsilon*OPT

key_findings.finding: Conjecture (not proven): influence maximization is NP-complete even for arborescences directed into a root. The general problem is already known NP-complete (cited to [3,4]) and APX-hard (cited to [3]).

limitations: Several proofs are deferred to a full version because of space constraints: Lemma 3 proof, and the extensions of the first-mover line algorithm to directed lines and outdirected arborescences (lines 168-171, 299-300).
The arborescence NP-completeness result is only conjectured (lines 59-60).
The FPTAS extension to bounded-treewidth graphs is asserted with a significant increase in complexity but not shown (lines 177-178).

The game has no pure-strategy Nash equilibria in general (lines 83-85), so equilibrium results rely on mixed strategies, and the reasoning about the price of competition relies on Vetta's theorem as cited.
Footnote 1 says more realistic marketing models reduce to the model here, citing [3]; this reduction is not argued in the text (lines 40-41).
The first-mover analysis is restricted to a duopoly with two players and to disjoint or directed line structures (Section 4).
No empirical evaluation, no real network data, and no computational experiments are reported.

summary_md:
Bharathi, Kempe and Salek extend the independent cascade model so that several players compete. Each player seeds a set of nodes. Every node adopts the first colour that reaches it, activation delays are exponentially distributed, and simultaneous arrivals are broken at random. The paper proves four things. (1) If the opponent's seeds are fixed, a player's expected reach is monotone and submodular in its own seeds, so greedy seeding achieves (1-1/e) of the best response. This holds only for the last player to commit. (2) Uncoordinated equilibria lose at most a factor of 2 against a single controller of all seeds (the price of competition). (3) Pure Nash equilibria need not exist, and the first-mover problem is solved only on disjoint lines. (4) An FPTAS exists for single-player influence maximization on bidirected trees. The paper is purely theoretical: it uses no data, estimates no parameters, and reports no experiments.

The paper matters because Melange explicitly names it as the basis of its A/B coalition cascade (scenario.py:6-12). The CU colour is A and the anti colour is B, where B is the anti-tier members plus neutrals mobilized by industry money with probability min(0.9, $/400k). The system cites the paper's last-mover submodularity result to justify lazy greedy and its non-additivity reporting.

Reading the code turned up three departures. None of these points has been reproduced by a second path, so all are UNVERIFIED (DE-062).
- **Tie-breaking:** the cascade advances in synchronous hops and always processes A nodes first, so pro-CU wins every same-hop tie. The paper uses continuous random delays with random tie-breaking.
- **Frontier greedy:** the budget frontier ranks seeds by marginal spread times a leverage or competitiveness factor, not by raw marginal spread, so the clean (1-1/e) guarantee on spread does not apply. Electoral mode also removes opponent seeds, which Lemma 1 does not cover.
- **Coalition allocator:** it water-fills money in proportion to single-seed marginals and runs no greedy at all.

The paper also leaves an open question for the system: industry is modelled as a fixed opponent that never responds to CU's choices. The paper shows that once the rival best-responds, guarantees exist only for lines.

bearings.paper_claim: Independent cascade extended to two colours. Each edge gets its activation coin and an exponential delay fixed before the run. Lemma 1 builds a deterministic equivalent in which each edge outcome is fixed in advance and a node takes the colour of the path that reaches it. The paper's random tie-breaking applies only when several players select the same seed node, not to simultaneous arrivals.

gaps_exposed: No opponent response: industry is an exogenous bystander-mobilization rate, never a strategic seeder. Under the paper's results, CU's greedy plan is a best response only if industry has already committed and will not react. The system has no first-mover or equilibrium analysis and no sensitivity test of a reacting rival.

The tie-break is hop-synchronous with A processed first, not random, so pro-CU wins every same-hop contest. The size of this bias is unmeasured. A CRN rerun with randomized or B-first frontier order would bound it.

The cascade has no timing model. The paper's exponential delays make arrival order depend on path timing, while the system uses unit hops. That affects who wins contested neutrals and cannot be calibrated, because the system has no join-timing data.

The (1-1/e) claim in scenario.py's docstring is broader than what the code satisfies. It holds only for coalition-mode frontier greedy with fac=1. It does not hold for leverage-weighted ranking, for contest plays that remove opponent seeds, or for the proportional water-fill coalition allocator.

The paper gives no empirical calibration: no edge probabilities, no saturation constant, and no money-to-seed mapping. The bystander rule min(0.9, $/400k) and the kernel constant 6 have no source in it.
flags: The brain notes (topics/2026-06-feature-cosponsor-and-sector-networks-june-network-plan.md:80,85) and scenario.py:9-12 say the coalition side is 'Submodular, so greedy (1-1/e)'. The code departs from the paper's conditions through deterministic A-first tie-breaking, leverage-weighted marginals, contest-seed removal, and proportional allocation in per_topic_coalition. The guarantee claim should be narrowed. This finding is UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
Expected spread is a heuristic model output. It is not a probability that members will join or a measure of access (D-025), and the paper has no legislative data to calibrate it.

The competitiveness multiplier enters the frontier's greedy ranking through fac. Its premise that dollars buy more in competitive seats is not validated (D-104..D-108), and the paper does not support it.
The paper proposes neither of the two rejected SNA changes (dropping regular cosponsorship edges; per-edge volume normalization). It does not use LDA as an edge source.
paul_alignment: The paper partly agrees with Paul's takeaway. He wants rival industries modelled explicitly (his margin note on Kim et al. 2025 about conflicting industries) and cheap scenario simulation (Fink). The paper gives the formal basis for treating rival industries as a competing colour, and the built Monte Carlo with common random numbers is a faithful live-edge implementation of the model. But Paul's notes treat competitive influence maximization as solved by greedy. The paper says greedy works only when the rival has already moved and will not react. If the rival responds, no pure equilibrium is guaranteed, and the first-mover problem is solved only on lines. Paul's position on this component should therefore record two caveats: industry is never strategic in the build, and the cascade breaks every tie in CU's favour. His Chen 2023 note that high-ranking pressure is 'not diminishing' challenges submodularity under linear-threshold contagion. It does not undercut the independent cascade result here, which is the regime Lemma 1 covers.
